claimed.text: Daniel Sheehan, who lobbied the conference, states that HPSCI Chairman Mike Turner first attacked the eminent domain provision and the Board's subpoena power and demanded both be removed. Turner and HASC Chairman Mike Rogers are named as leading the effort, with support from Mitch McConnell and Speaker Mike Johnson. Sheehan is the only named participant to describe the demands, and no conference document names who struck what.
The Debrief reported the dilution in conference at the time as a deliberate weakening rather than a drafting accident.

Schumer said Americans have a right to learn about technologies of unknown origins and non-human intelligence, framed the Act as carrying on Harry Reid's legacy, and called it an outrage that the House did not work with the Senate on the review board.

Rounds said a central collection and a reputable review board would add to the credibility of future investigations, and announced at the 2026 Disclosure Symposium that he was once again cosponsoring the Act as an NDAA amendment.

On the board's reading the Act's definitions of legacy program and controlling authority were drafted in response to Grusch's published allegations, 38 days earlier, and the provisions removed in conference were exactly the machinery that would have moved custody or compelled testimony.

The board reads the pattern of what was cut and kept as a jurisdictional defence of the armed services and intelligence committees, and treats Sheehan's account as the working hypothesis until conference records are released.

contested.text: Turner has said that the whistleblowers repeatedly had to say they did not actually have any knowledge.

AARO's Historical Record Report attributes the reverse-engineering claim to circular reporting, asserts that none of its interviewees had firsthand knowledge, and says the companies named by interviewees denied the programmes to its director.

The board's entry for Sheehan, the one named source for the conference account, records that in Avirgan v. Hull the court dismissed the suit in 1988 and ordered the Christic Institute to pay fees and costs under Rule 11, and Sheehan also represents Luis Elizondo in a case against the Defense Department.

The records describe the Senate text differently: the engrossed S. 2226 carries it as Division G, sections 9001 to 9015, while other entries describe Division I of H.R. 2670 with sections 9001 to 9010 and place the legacy program definition at section 9001(11).
The records disagree on whether the House adopted the 2026 amendment on 22 or 23 July.

lead.text: The UAP Disclosure Act, filed by Chuck Schumer with five cosponsors on 13 July 2023 and passed by the Senate inside its FY2024 NDAA on 27 July, would have created an independent Records Review Board and ordered the government to take by eminent domain any recovered technologies of unknown origin held by private parties. Conference removed both; what became law is a records collection at the National Archives.

questions: Who in the FY2024 conference struck the Review Board and the eminent domain clause, and will the conference records ever be released?
Has Turner confirmed or denied Sheehan's account of what he demanded?
Why did Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich not sign the 2024 refiling?
Why has no committee ever marked up the Act, and why did Schumer never speak for it on the floor the day he filed it?
Will the Senate take up the House-adopted successor, and will its contractor reach survive conference?
Where does testimony from legacy program personnel go now that the Board that was to receive it does not exist?

record.text: S.Amdt. 797 was submitted on 13 July 2023 by Schumer for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, ordered to lie on the table and printed in the Congressional Record at pages S2953 to S2959; its action record shows three actions that day and no vote.
The amendment travelled into S. 2226 as Division G, sections 9001 to 9015, which the Senate passed on 27 July 2023.

Its findings say legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that UAP records exist that have not been declassified, in part because of Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an over-broad reading of transclassified foreign nuclear information. It defines non-human intelligence as any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin.

Section 9007 established the Records Review Board as an independent agency of nine citizens appointed by the President with Senate consent, barred anyone with any involvement in a legacy program or controlling authority, drew nominations from congressional leaders, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, nonprofit UAP research organisations and the American Historical Association, and required disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence for postponement.

Section 9010(a) reads: "The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good." The material was to go to the Board at a location suitable to its controlling authority, the Board was to decide whether it met that description beyond a reasonable doubt, and it was to have access to testimony from legacy program personnel.

Section 9009(c)(3) required the Board to produce a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, a benchmark-driven schedule for the disclosure of postponed items including recovered technologies, and to brief AARO on it before terminating; section 9014 authorised $20,000,000.

The enacted Public Law 118-31 contains no occurrence of Review Board or eminent domain; sections 9007 to 9011, 9013 and 9014 have no enacted counterpart, and only sections 1841 to 1843 survived. No enacted statute mentions a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan.
In enacted law the postponement judgement the Board would have made belongs to the original classification authority, the offices the Board was created to review.

The Board's nomination route ran through congressional leadership and outside bodies, never through the intelligence committees; the enacted section 1841(e)(2) instead gives HPSCI, House Oversight and House Armed Services continuing oversight of the collection.
Jack Reed introduced the Senate vehicle and signed the conference product that removed his chamber's division. Warner's contractor turn-in, which passed the Senate the same day, was removed with it.

On 11 July 2024 Rounds, for himself and Schumer, filed the complete Act again, eminent domain clause intact, as S.Amdt. 2610 to the FY2025 NDAA; it was ordered to lie on the table and never called up. Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich were not on it, and the enacted FY2025 act contains no disclosure division.

Burlison said that the Act had been stripped out by the House the year before and that he could not get it onto that year's House bill; the FY2026 act again contains no eminent domain, non-human or legacy program language.
The Senate Armed Services Committee's FY2027 bill as reported under Roger Wicker contains no UAP provisions, and Rounds's own list of provisions he secured in it has no UAP item.
The New Paradigm Institute, led by Daniel Sheehan, runs a campaign headed The House Acted. Now Tell the Senate to Pass the UAPDA.

summary.text: The Act's findings rest on the premise that UAP records exist that have not been declassified, and its definitions of non-human intelligence, legacy program and controlling authority presuppose programmes and private holders of recovered material.

It was never marked up by a committee or introduced as a freestanding bill; it travelled only as a floor amendment, was refiled in 2024, when it was ordered to lie on the table, and was announced again in 2026.
In July 2026 the House adopted Eric Burlison's successor amendment, with a Senate-confirmed review board and reach to contractors, against a Senate FY2027 bill that carries no UAP provisions.

title: The UAP Disclosure Act and what survived it
